summary: Tipaza, the capital of Algeria’s Tipaza Province, was known as Tipasa under Roman rule and developed from a Punic trading-post into a military colony and Christian hub with three basilicas. The modern town was founded in 1857 and is a tourism destination for its ancient ruins and sandy littoral, while a nearby transmitter broadcasts French-language Channel 3 programs on 252 kHz.

coreControversy.regulatoryOrHistoricalPrecedent: Tipasa developed from a Punic trading-post into a Roman military colony under Claudius, subsequently becoming the municipium Colonia Aelia Tipasensis; destruction by the Vandals in 430 CE was followed by Byzantine reconstruction one century later and demolition by Umayyad forces at the end of the seventh century.

hiddenCatchesAndLimits: The modern town founded in 1857 represents resettlement after the ancient city’s destruction, rather than an uninterrupted survival of the Roman settlement.
The population of 20,000 inhabitants refers to the fourth century and is attributed to Stéphane Gsell; nearly 30,000 inhabitants describes the modern town.
The transmitter’s reported return to broadcasting followed an outage beginning March 17, 2014, so its service history includes an interruption.
Tipaza and its surroundings are home to the Chenoua people, described as the largest Berber-speaking group of western Algeria; the majority of the Bouriba family also reside in this area.

avoidAdvice: Do not conflate the fourth-century population estimate of 20,000 inhabitants with the modern description of nearly 30,000 inhabitants.
fitAdvice: Tipaza combines provincial-capital status, tourism centered on ancient Tipasa’s ruins, and a nearby French-language Channel 3 longwave service on 252 kHz.
